dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — A walk in Plaka
dialogs.intro: Eleni shows Ana around the foot of the Acropolis. Notice that the same adjective appears in three different outfits in this dialogue — and that the outfit is always chosen by the noun next to it.

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: What a beautiful day! The weather is wonderful today.
lines.literal: what — beautiful (fem.) — day! the — weather — it-is — wonderful (masc.) — today.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Yes, very hot. Look, what a pretty house!
lines.literal: yes, very — hot (masc.). look, what — pretty (neut.) — house!

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: It's an old house. Plaka is an old neighborhood.
lines.literal: it-is — old (neut.) — house. the — Plaka — it-is — an — old (fem.) — neighborhood.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: And these shops are small but nice.
lines.literal: and — these (neut. pl.) — the (pl.) — shops — they-are — small (neut. pl.) — but — beautiful (neut. pl.).

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: Do you want an iced coffee? The coffee here is very good.
lines.literal: you-want — a (masc.) — freddo? here — the — coffee — it-is — very — good (masc.).

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: OK. Oh, what's this big church?
lines.literal: OK. ah, what — it-is — this (fem.) — the — big (fem.) — church?

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: It's an old Byzantine church. Very famous.
lines.literal: it-is — an — old (fem.) — Byzantine (fem.) — church. very — famous (fem.).

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: And noisy! But yes, it's wonderful.
lines.literal: and — noisy! but — yes, it-is — wonderful (fem.).

notes: **One adjective, three endings.** υπέροχ**ος** καιρός, υπέροχ**η** πόλη, υπέροχ**ο** σπίτι. ⚠️ For English speakers this is genuinely new work: in English "great" never changes, whether it describes a house, a city, or a coffee. In Greek it changes every time.

**Luckily, the ending echoes the article.** **ο** → -**ος**, **η** → -**η**, **το** → -**ο**. When in doubt, look at the noun's article and copy its sound: ο καφές → καλ**ός**, η μέρα → καλ**ή**, το νερό → καλ**ό**. This simple trick works about nine times out of ten.

**The adjective goes IN FRONT of the noun**, just as in English. "Old house" is *παλιό σπίτι*. ⚠️ Putting it after isn't fatally wrong, but it changes the feel: *το σπίτι το παλιό* sounds like you're picking out one house among several.

**An adjective can stand in two places, with different meanings.** *Το σπίτι είναι παλιό* = "the house is old" (a statement). *Το παλιό σπίτι* = "the old house" (a label). The first is a full sentence, the second only part of one — exactly like English.

⚠️ **After αυτός, the article stays.** *αυτή **η** εκκλησία*, *αυτά **τα** μαγαζιά*, *αυτό **το** σπίτι*. To English ears this sounds doubled — "this the church" — but dropping the article is a mistake people hear immediately. Learn the chunks: **αυτός ο**, **αυτή η**, **αυτό το**.
**Πολύ means "very" and never changes** when it modifies an adjective: πολύ καλός, πολύ καλή, πολύ καλό. It only changes when it means "much / many" in front of a noun — and that's for later units.

**Τι ωραία μέρα! is the standard exclamation pattern**: Τι + adjective + noun, with no article — just like English "What a…!". Τι ωραίο σπίτι! Τι όμορφη πόλη! Τι καλός άνθρωπος! This pattern is free and sounds natural right away.

**Φρέντο εσπρέσο and φρέντο καπουτσίνο are the two national drinks of modern Greece** — espresso and cappuccino shaken with ice. Ordering *ελληνικός καφές* (Greek coffee boiled in a briki) always earns a warm welcome too, but be warned: the grounds stay in the cup — don't drink the last sip.

grammars.title: Adjective endings: six boxes that cover A1
body: Most Greek adjectives follow the pattern of καλός. Learn this one word properly, and hundreds of others come along for free.
after: ⚠️ A group of adjectives uses **-α** instead of -η in the feminine, namely those whose stem ends in a vowel or ρ: ωραί**α**, νέ**α**, παλι**ά**, μικρ**ή** but κρύ**α**. Your ear will find it faster than the rule; when in doubt, use -η.

A few common adjectives have their own pattern, for example **πολύς, πολλή, πολύ** (much, many) and **θορυβώδης, θορυβώδης, θορυβώδες** (noisy). Don't memorize them now — just recognize them when you meet them.

grammars.title: Two positions, two meanings
body: The difference is small on the page but big to the ear, and once you get it, your sentences immediately sound more Greek.
after: ⚠️ The last row has four words before the noun appears, and all of them are masculine. If even one is in the wrong outfit, the whole string sounds lopsided. Practice by naming the things around you out loud: *αυτό το μεγάλο τραπέζι*, *αυτή η μικρή πόρτα*.

blocks.title: Four colors that refuse to change
items: **μπλε, γκρι, καφέ, ροζ** were borrowed whole from French and never take Greek endings: *το μπλε σπίτι*, *η μπλε πόρτα*, *οι μπλε πόρτες*. Four free words.
⚠️ **καφέ** means "brown" **and** "coffee" — but the coffee is **ο καφές** with ς, the color is **καφέ** without ς. One letter separates a "brown door" from a "coffee door".
For the sea and the sky, Greeks use **γαλάζιος** (*ghah-LAH-zee-ohs*, light blue) more often than μπλε. The Greek flag is γαλάζιο, not μπλε.
